title: Τράγος καὶ ἄμπελος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 339. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Τράγος ἐν τῇ ἐκβολῇ τῆς ἀμπέλου τὴν βλάστην ἔτρωγε.
sentences.tr: Tragos en tēi ekbolēi tēs ampelou tēn blastēn etrōge.
sentences.l: A goat, at the vine's putting-forth, was gnawing the new growth.
sentences.i: At the season when the vine was putting out its shoots, a goat was gnawing the new growth.
sentences.n: ἐκβολή is the throwing-out of the shoots, the vine's budding, and so marks the time of year as much as the place. ἔτρωγε is imperfect: he was at it steadily, not once.

sentences.t: Τούτῳ δὲ προσεῖπεν ἡ ἄμπελος· « Τί με βλάπτεις ;
sentences.tr: Toutōi de proseipen hē ampelos· « Ti me blapteis ;
sentences.l: And the vine said to him: « Why do you harm me?
sentences.n: The speech runs on into the next line, so this sentence opens its quotation marks and does not close them — an established pattern in this collection where Chambry's punctuation divides a speech. His French typography also sets a space before the Greek question mark, and it is kept as printed.

sentences.l: For surely it is not that there is no grass?
sentences.n: μή in a question expects the answer 'no', and the οὐκ inside it presses the point: 'surely it is not the case that there is no grass?' The vine's answer is that grass is there in plenty, and the goat has no need of her.

sentences.t: Ὅμως ὅσον σοῦ θυομένου οἶνον χρῄζουσιν, ἐγὼ παρέξω. »
sentences.tr: Homōs hoson sou thyomenou oinon chrēizousin, egō parexō. »
sentences.l: All the same, as much wine as they need when you are being sacrificed, I shall supply. »
sentences.i: All the same, I shall furnish the wine they need at your sacrifice. »
sentences.n: σοῦ θυομένου is a genitive absolute — 'you being sacrificed' — one of the commonest joints in these fables. The goat was the beast offered to Dionysos, the god of the vine, and the wine poured over the victim would be hers: the vine is promising to be present at his death.

sentences.t: Τοὺς ἀχαρίστους καὶ βουλομένους τοὺς φίλους πλεονεκτεῖν ὁ μῦθος ἐλέγχει.
sentences.tr: Tous acharistous kai boulomenous tous philous pleonektein ho mythos elenchei.
sentences.l: The ungrateful, and those wishing to get-the-better-of their friends, the fable exposes.
sentences.i: The fable exposes the ungrateful, and those who wish to take advantage of their friends.
sentences.n: A closing formula met elsewhere in the collection, ὁ μῦθος ἐλέγχει (as at fable 93, fable 227 and fable 288): ἐλέγχω is the courtroom word, to put a man to the proof and so show him up. πλεονεκτέω is to claim more than one's share, and takes the accusative of the person overreached.
